dm: Subhūti, what do you think?
gm: "Subhūti, what do you think?

dm: Do you think, Subhūti, that there is any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
gm: Do you think there is any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as the unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening?"

dm: The venerable Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
gm: The venerable Subhūti said, "Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as the unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening."

dm: The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, it is so. It is just so."
gm: The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, so it is, so it is.

dm: For there is not the slightest dharma to be conceptually observed or to exist.
gm: In it, not even the slightest dharma is apprehended or exists;

dm: Therefore, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
gm: therefore it is called 'unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening.'

dm: Furthermore, Subhūti, that dharma is equal;
gm: Furthermore, Subhūti, that dharma is equal;

dm: Since there is nothing whatsoever that is unequal or equal, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
gm: because there is nothing whatsoever unequal or equal in it, therefore it is called 'unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening'."

dm: That unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is equal in being without a self, without a sentient being, without a life-force, and without a person;
gm: That unexcelled, perfectly complete awakening is equal in being without a self, without a sentient being, without a living soul, and without a person;

dm: it is perfectly and completely awakened through all wholesome dharmas.
gm: it is fully awakened to by means of all wholesome dharmas.

dm: Subhūti, as for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata has taught that they are devoid of the nature of dharmas;
gm: Subhūti, as for what are called 'wholesome dharmas', the Tathāgata has spoken of them as being exactly non-dharmas;

dm: therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas."
gm: therefore they are called 'wholesome dharmas'.

dm: Furthermore, Subhūti, if any son or daughter of noble family were to gather a heap of the seven precious substances equal in size to as many Mount Merus, the kings of mountains, as there are in the trichiliocosm, and give them as a gift, and if another person were to take from this Perfection of Wisdom even just a four-line stanza and teach it to others, Subhūti, that former heap of merit would not approach even a hundredth part of the latter, nor would it bear comparison, even up to the point of calculation.
gm: Furthermore, Subhūti, compared to any son of noble family or daughter of noble family who, having collected heaps of the seven precious substances equal in amount to however many Sumerus, kings of mountains, there are in the three thousand grand thousand world systems, gives them as a gift, if someone were to take up even just a single four-line stanza from this perfection of wisdom and teach it to others, Subhūti, that former heap of merit does not approach even a hundredth part of this one, up to not even bearing comparison.

dm: Subhūti, what do you think?
gm: Subhūti, what do you think of this?

dm: If you think that the Tathāgata considers, "I have liberated sentient beings," Subhūti, do not view it in that way.
gm: If you think the Tathāgata intends, 'I shall liberate sentient beings,' Subhūti, it should not be seen like that.

dm: Why is that? Subhūti, it is because there are no sentient beings whatsoever that have been liberated by the Tathāgata.
gm: Why is that? Because, Subhūti, there are no sentient beings whatsoever who are liberated by the Tathāgata.

dm: Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to liberate any sentient being whatsoever, that would be the Tathāgata grasping at a self.
gm: Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to have liberated any sentient beings whatsoever, that itself would be an apprehension of a self by the Tathāgata,

dm: It would be grasping at a sentient being, grasping at a life-force, and grasping at a person.
gm: an apprehension of a sentient being, an apprehension of a living soul, and an apprehension of a person.

dm: Subhūti, what is called "grasping at a self" has been declared by the Tathāgata to be "non-grasping," yet it is grasped by immature ordinary beings.
gm: Subhūti, as for what is called 'apprehension of a self', the Tathāgata has spoken of it as non-apprehension; yet it is apprehended by childish ordinary beings.

dm: Subhūti, as for what are called "immature ordinary beings," the Tathāgata has declared them to be non-beings.
gm: Subhūti, as for what are called 'childish ordinary beings', the Tathāgata has spoken of them as being exactly non-beings;

dm: Therefore, they are called "immature ordinary beings."
gm: therefore they are called 'childish ordinary beings'.

dm: Subhūti, what do you think?
gm: Subhūti, what do you think of this?

dm: Do you think that the Tathāgata should be seen by means of his perfect marks?
gm: Do you think that the Tathāgata is to be seen by the perfection of his marks?

dm: Subhūti replied, "No, Blessed One, it is not so."
gm: Subhūti said, 'Blessed One, it is not so.'

dm: "The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his perfect marks."
gm: The Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of his marks.'

dm: The Blessed One replied, "Subhūti, it is so. It is just so.
gm: The Blessed One said, 'Subhūti, it is so. It is exactly so;

dm: The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his perfect marks.
gm: the Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of his marks.

dm: Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to be seen by means of his perfect marks, then a wheel-turning monarch would also be a Tathāgata."
gm: Subhūti, if the Tathāgata were to be seen by the perfection of his marks, a wheel-turning king would also be a Tathāgata;

dm: Therefore, the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his perfect marks.
gm: therefore, the Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of his marks.'

dm: Then, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One in this way:
gm: Then the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the Blessed One:

dm: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his perfect marks."
gm: 'Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, the Tathāgata is not to be seen by the perfection of his marks.'
